extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and argumentation
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for assessing the strength, scope, and legitimacy of inductive/generalizing arguments (when approximate generalizations may be treated as reliable, how probabilities combine, and how mathematical and geometric truths differ in status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution of probability when chaining approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When several 'most A are B' style premises are chained, the probability of the final conclusion diminishes multiplicatively — the error of the conclusion will amount to the aggregate of the errors of all the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated numerically: if 'most A are B' is 9/10 and 'most B are C' is 8/9, then proportion of A that are C is 8/10; adding 'most C are D' at 7/8 yields 7/10. Experience rarely allows precise numerical estimation of each step's diminution, so remember probability diminishes at every step and unless premises are nearly universal the conclusion after few steps is worth little; hearsay-of-a-hearsay is worthless at a few removes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform approximate generalizations into universal propositions with provisos when exceptions are known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason for stopping at an approximate generalization is inconvenience rather than impossibility, and we know the character of exceptions, we may substitute a universal proposition with an explicit proviso (condition) recording the exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Most persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill' → 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose.' Carrying the proviso forward in reasoning lets one treat the premise as universal while tracking exactly how far conclusions depart from universal applicability. When multiple such conditioned universals are combined, their conditions sum to show aggregate error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations valid as universals for inquiries about multitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: For sciences concerned with the properties of masses (e.g., politics, human society), what is true of most individuals can be treated as if true of the whole mass for practical and scientific purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statesmen and social scientists can reason and act as if what is true of most persons were true of all when arranging for large groups or indefinite successions of individuals; thus approximate truths about individuals yield practically absolute results when applied to masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence claims: inference from perception or inductive connection
rubrics_metrics.description: In logical induction, 'existence' refers to phenomena as perceived or to the inferred possibility of perceiving them; existence of an individual phenomenon not directly perceived is inferred from its inductive connections (succession or co-existence) with known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General propositions affirming bare existence can be established by a single positive instance (e.g., if a unicorn were positively seen once, its existence would be fully established). We prove existence by showing connection by succession/co-existence with known things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of resemblance via a third object when direct juxtaposition is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: When two objects cannot be directly compared, the scientific method is to compare each to a third object (a transported standard) and infer their resemblance or difference through that intermediary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: use a foot-rule applied to each line in turn; logical formula cited: 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another.' Many resemblance judgments require minute, part-by-part comparison; apparent similarity can hide real differences unless carefully inspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical laws of resemblance are independent of causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The only laws of resemblance requiring independent treatment are mathematical (axioms about equality, inequality, proportionality); other resemblances among physical phenomena are derived from or identical with laws of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: equality of angles of reflection is identical with the causal law producing the effect, while axioms like 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' hold irrespective of causal origin and therefore belong to mathematics rather than empirical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order in place (collocation) is generally consequence of causal laws; geometry is exceptional
rubrics_metrics.description: Order in place of effects is typically a consequence of the laws of their causes; the only general propositions about order in place independent of causation are geometric truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, apart from geometry (where positional relations can be inferred independently of physical causes), order-in-place facts are treated by referencing the causal laws that produced them. Geometry and mathematics therefore require separate methodological inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental arithmetic axioms are inductive truths grounded in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary axioms of arithmetic (e.g., 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equal to one another', 'Equals added to equals make equal sums') are inductive truths based on continual observation and hence form the base premises of numerical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers denote physical aggregates; the meanings of number-names connote physical modes of formation of aggregates. The law 'the sums of equals are equals' justifies arithmetical operations and is considered an inductive law of the highest order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra and higher mathematics proceed deductively from axioms and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraical theorems and theorems of higher mathematics are derived deductively: given basic axioms and definitions, one demonstrates results by pure ratiocination applying those axioms at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example problem: express what function (a+b)^n will be of a and b (binomial theorem). While the axioms are inductive in origin, the bulk of mathematical reasoning is deductive from those starting premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical comparison of ideas can substitute for comparison of phenomena when ideas fully represent phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics, comparison is often between ideas rather than outward phenomena, but this is acceptable only when the idea is a complete picture of the phenomenon with respect to the matter in hand (e.g., numbers, lines, figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence explains why some mathematical truths appear to be known by 'intuition' or 'instinct', but it does not generalize to empirical sciences where ideas do not fully capture the causal or experimental aspects of phenomena (e.g., contemplating gunpowder won't reveal its explosive property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a uniform mode of formation for numbers to enable generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: To reason about numbers generally (leading to algebra), it is sufficient to select one consistent mode of formation for each number (e.g., successor +1) so that all other modes can be deduced; this supports the development of general functions and algebraic notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via modes of formation (e.g., 6 = 4 + 2, etc.). The algebraic nomenclature (a, b, n) expresses modes of formation abstractly and facilitates general theorems about functions of numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and carry forward conditions to account for aggregate error in composed arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When substituting conditioned universals for approximate premises, explicitly record each proviso/condition and carry them forward so the final conclusion is qualified by the aggregate of those conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example combining: 'Most persons with uncontrolled power...' + 'All absolute monarchs have uncontrolled power, unless...' → conclude 'All absolute monarchs employ their power ill, unless [condition A] or [condition B].' How rapidly errors accumulate then ceases to matter provided each error/condition is tracked.
